snippet.title: When Plane Landings Turned into Deadly Disasters
snippet.description:
In this gripping, action-packed investigation, we break down three routine landing approaches that instantly evolved into terrifying survival scenarios and catastrophic crashes. Discover how Garuda Flight 200 slammed down at a blazingly fast 250 mph because the captain became completely fixated on a manual checklist, leaving the flaps at an unsafe 5 degrees and ignoring 15 ground proximity alerts before bouncing into an 1,800° swampy inferno. Then, we witness the raw, unpredictable force of nature as a veteran Delta crew battles a violent microburst in 101-degree heat, dropping their massive Tristar a mile short of the runway at 200 mph, leaving only 27 survivors. Finally, we deconstruct the automation paradox behind Asiana Flight 214, exposing how an intricate sequence of autopilot inputs accidentally forced a modern jetliner into an unrecoverable glide. Through real cockpit voice recorders, high-risk simulation tests, and definitive physical evidence, see how investigators uncovered the dark truth behind these ultimate landing disasters.

snippet.title: Why Our Solar System Is More Dangerous Than You Think
snippet.description:

Now, through the lenses of our most intrepid space probes, we are pulling back the curtain on the solar system’s most volatile, high-stakes environments. From the hellish, 460°C toxic greenhouse of Venus to the colossal 24-kilometer peaks of Olympus Mons on Mars, this extreme documentary explores the ultimate wonders of science. Witness how robotic pioneers like Voyager 2 and Cassini braved violent cosmic anomalies, catastrophic solar flares, and crushing air pressures to reveal hidden oceans locked beneath kilometers of alien ice. Discover the brutal 4.5-billion-year history of our cosmic neighborhood and uncover the terrifying secrets of the universe that dictate the past, present, and future of planet Earth.

snippet.title: Air France 736: They Climbed With a Massive Fuel Leak and No One Stopped Them
snippet.description:
Air France Flight 736: The Fuel Leak That Almost Turned an A330 Into a Fireball

In this video, we uncover the terrifying chain of events behind Air France Flight 736, an Airbus A330 that lifted off from Brazzaville on New Year's Eve 2020, heading to Paris. What began as a normal overnight flight slowly turned into a hidden emergency in cruise. A tiny maintenance detail, buried inside the left engine, started draining tonnes of fuel into the air and pushed the aircraft closer and closer to a disaster that should have ended in flames.

The most shocking part is not the leak itself. It is how an experienced crew, with thousands of hours, repeatedly chose to override the checklist and trust their instincts instead.

Why did they keep the leaking engine running?
Why did they land with boiling hot brakes while fuel was pouring out nearby?
And how did this flight not end in a runway inferno?

📚 Related Videos
Emirates Flight Investigation: https://youtu.be/1zdtquGc7wQ

Singapore Airlines : https://youtu.be/xZLOg0XybIY

South Korean Airline Flight Disaster: https://youtu.be/lOeiTgP2Tpk

✈️ The Incident

After recent heavy maintenance in China, the A330 departed Brazzaville with 136 passengers, three pilots, eight cabin crew, and two maintenance technicians on board. Engine number one had a hidden problem. A fuel hose flange was not correctly mounted, which slowly turned a simple fitting into a dangerous leak.

At first, everything looked normal. Takeoff was smooth. The climb to flight level 380 was uneventful. Then the captain did the first fuel check and noticed something wrong. About 1.4 tonnes of fuel appeared to be missing. Minutes later, the loss grew, a fuel imbalance formed, and all signs pointed to a leak on the left side.

The paper fuel leak checklist was opened. The very first line was clear. Land as soon as possible and shut down the engine on the suspected leak side. But the crew hesitated. They had alternates nearby. They still had plenty of fuel. They did not like the idea of shutting down an engine at cruise. So they tried to manage the situation on their own terms.

Fuel kept leaking. The imbalance increased. The aircraft continued flying north. The closer they got to N'Djamena, the more they convinced themselves that they could keep both engines running until landing.

🔥 The Investigation

When the aircraft finally diverted to N'Djamena, the danger was at its peak. The A330 was landing on a shorter runway, with a strong tailwind, flaps 3, higher speed, and a leaking engine that had already lost more than 5 tonnes of fuel.

Heavy braking pushed the brake temperature up toward 300 degrees, then 600 degrees after taxi. At the same time, fuel was still pouring from engine one, flowing in exactly the area where overheated brakes could have ignited it instantly.


Airbus had already identified the flange design issue years earlier. The updated part existed, but the older design was still being used. The BEA concluded that the maintenance error created the leak, but the real danger came from human decisions in the cockpit.

The only reason this did not turn into an in-flight fire or runway fireball was a rare fuel concentration around the leak that was too rich to ignite. That was not skill. It was luck.

📌 In this video, we break down:

How a misfitted fuel hose on an A330 led to a massive leak

Why the crew ignored multiple checklist steps to shut down the engine

How tailwind, hot brakes, and leaking fuel created a perfect fire scenario

What investigators found in the fuel system and maintenance history

Why Airbus changed the hardware and procedures after the incident

How Air France's cockpit culture came under fire in the final report

What this near disaster teaches about human factors and overconfidence in aviation

If you are fascinated by aviation incidents, cockpit decision making, and real crash investigations, this breakdown will show you how close Flight 736 came to becoming another headline tragedy.

What actually happened to the ancient Maya? Mysteries unfold in this four episode Rise and Fall of the Maya Mega Episode compilation from National Geographic. Journey where the Maya lived in Mexico and Guatemala as archaeologists and historians uncover new evidence that rewrites what we know about this fascinating and mysterious ancient civilization. From the monumental discovery of a 3,000-year-old hidden megastructure to the puzzling, catastrophic collapse that forced millions to abandon their pyramid-filled cities, explore the origins of Maya power, secrets, and resilience in this documentary series. Featuring full episodes: 

Origins - 00:00 
What is Aguada Fénix? In June 2020, scientists discover Aguada Fénix, a monumental 3,000-year-old Maya structure. Uncover the hidden secrets of Aguada Fénix, the oldest monument built by the ancient Maya civilization, dating back to around 1000 BCE, that challenge everything we knew about the Maya's earliest days.

Civilization - 44:03 
New architectural and technological evidence unearthed in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula transforms long-held ideas about how the Maya civilization grew into a superpower.

Collapse - 01:28:06
Why did the ancient Maya civilization collapse? Many cities were abandoned due to a complex combination of severe droughts, overpopulation, deforestation, and warfare. The exact series of events that lead the ancient Maya to abandon their pyramid-filled cities has long puzzled archaeologists. Now, new investigations in Mexico and Guatemala are exposing surprising evidence about why these great monuments were deserted. 

Resilience - 02:12:09
Archaeologists unearth new clues about the resurgence of the ancient Maya civilization and the devastating events that would ultimately lead them to abandon their cities for good. Investigations also reveal evidence of extreme resilience in the face of catastrophe.

snippet.description:
In this episode of Mayday Air Disaster: The Accident Files, examine three fateful decisions in the cockpit that turned minor mechanical issues into catastrophic, history-altering aviation accidents. Inside the Fateful Decisions Covered in This Video:

TransAsia Flight 235: A faulty circuit board sensor triggers a false engine flameout warning over Taipei. In a tragic case of change blindness, the captain accidentally shuts down the plane's only functioning engine, sending the aircraft into the Keelung River.

KLM Cityhopper Flight 433: Misinterpreting a false oil pressure light, the crew pulls a healthy engine back to idle. During a low-altitude go-around at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport, an uncoordinated thrust imbalance forces the turboprop into a fatal right bank.

Virgin Galactic SpaceShipTwo: During a high-speed rocket test flight over the Mojave Desert, a time-crunch panic causes the co-pilot to prematurely unlock the craft’s unique feathering system, allowing severe aerodynamic forces to tear the experimental spaceship apart.

Discover the harrowing chain of events behind these air disasters, the lessons learned by air crash investigators, and why aviation experts stress that a checklist is the most powerful tool a pilot has to survive a crisis.

For the past four months, Kenya has been dealing with the fallout of a shocking story. It centres around a televangelist - Paul Mackenzie - who reportedly led hundreds of his followers to their deaths by telling them that the world was coming to an end.

Should the authorities have done more to contain Mackenzie’s doomsday preachings? If so, how would that square with the right - constitutionally protected in Kenya - to freedom of speech and religion?

snippet.title: Air France Flight 011:The Boeing 777 Wasn’t Broken, The Pilots Were Fighting Each Other
snippet.description:
✈️ Air France Flight 011, The Boeing 777 That Started Fighting Itself

In this video, we break down the strange and terrifying story of Air France Flight 011, a Boeing 777-300ER that came within seconds of a serious loss-of-control event during a go-around at Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport.

The aircraft was healthy.
The pilots were experienced.
The systems were working normally.
There was no turbulence, no 5G interference, no flight control failure, and no mechanical fault.

Yet just over 1,000 feet above the ground, on final approach to Paris, the Boeing 777 suddenly began behaving in a way the pilots could not explain.

The controls felt stiff.
The aircraft pitched up sharply.
The cockpit filled with alarms.
Air traffic control heard the pilots struggling over the radio.

And for 53 seconds, two highly trained pilots were unknowingly fighting each other inside a perfectly functioning airplane.

How can a Boeing 777 feel broken when nothing has failed?

And how can two experienced pilots both believe they are saving the aircraft, while actually making the situation worse?

📚 Related Videos

Emirates Flight Investigation: https://youtu.be/1zdtquGc7wQ

Singapore Airlines: https://youtu.be/xZLOg0XybIY

South Korean Airline Flight Disaster: https://youtu.be/lOeiTgP2Tpk

✈️ The Story

Air France Flight 011 was a scheduled overnight flight from New York JFK to Paris Charles de Gaulle on April 5, 2022.

The Boeing 777-300ER, registration F-GSQJ, was carrying 177 passengers and 15 crew members. After crossing the Atlantic through the night, the aircraft was lined up for an ILS approach to runway 26L at Charles de Gaulle.

The weather was gray, cloudy, and rainy, but still within limits. The crew had planned a normal landing.

But during the final approach, the first officer noticed what felt like unusual banking behavior. The aircraft appeared to be drifting, and with no outside visual reference in the clouds, his concern quickly grew.

At just over 1,100 feet, he called for a go-around.

A go-around is supposed to be the safe decision. Power up, pitch up, climb away, and try again.

But this go-around began with the aircraft already banked left. The first officer pitched the nose up aggressively, while the captain, seeing the pitch increasing too fast, instinctively pushed forward on his own control column to stop it.

That single moment changed everything.

Now both pilots were flying at the same time.

On an Airbus, the cockpit would announce a “dual input” warning. But on the Boeing 777, there is no such voice alert. Instead, the control columns are physically linked, and the aircraft follows the average of both pilots’ inputs.

When the opposing forces became strong enough, the Boeing 777’s breakout mechanism activated. This system is designed to help pilots if one control column jams. But in this case, nothing had jammed.

Even worse, the captain was accidentally transmitting parts of the cockpit struggle over the radio, allowing air traffic control to hear the confusion live.

But the aircraft was not broken.

The Boeing 777 was doing exactly what it had been designed to do.

📌 In this video, we cover

• The full timeline of Air France Flight 011
• Why the Boeing 777 go-around became so dangerous

✈️ Air France Flight 011, The Boeing 777 That Started Fighting Itself

In this video, we break down the strange and terrifying story of Air France Flight 011, a Boeing 777-300ER that came within seconds of a serious loss-of-control event during a go-around at Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport.

The aircraft was healthy.
The pilots were experienced.
The systems were working normally.
There was no turbulence, no 5G interference, no flight control failure, and no mechanical fault.

Yet just over 1,000 feet above the ground, on final approach to Paris, the Boeing 777 suddenly began behaving in a way the pilots could not explain.

The controls felt stiff.
The aircraft pitched up sharply.
The cockpit filled with alarms.
Air traffic control heard the pilots struggling over the radio.

And for 53 seconds, two highly trained pilots were unknowingly fighting each other inside a perfectly functioning airplane.

How can a Boeing 777 feel broken when nothing has failed?

And how can two experienced pilots both believe they are saving the aircraft, while actually making the situation worse?

✈️ The Story

Air France Flight 011 was a scheduled overnight flight from New York JFK to Paris Charles de Gaulle on April 5, 2022.

The Boeing 777-300ER, registration F-GSQJ, was carrying 177 passengers and 15 crew members. After crossing the Atlantic through the night, the aircraft was lined up for an ILS approach to runway 26L at Charles de Gaulle.

The weather was gray, cloudy, and rainy, but still within limits. The crew had planned a normal landing.

But during the final approach, the first officer noticed what felt like unusual banking behavior. The aircraft appeared to be drifting, and with no outside visual reference in the clouds, his concern quickly grew.

At just over 1,100 feet, he called for a go-around.

A go-around is supposed to be the safe decision. Power up, pitch up, climb away, and try again.

But this go-around began with the aircraft already banked left. The first officer pitched the nose up aggressively, while the captain, seeing the pitch increasing too fast, instinctively pushed forward on his own control column to stop it.

That single moment changed everything.

Now both pilots were flying at the same time.

On an Airbus, the cockpit would announce a “dual input” warning. But on the Boeing 777, there is no such voice alert. Instead, the control columns are physically linked, and the aircraft follows the average of both pilots’ inputs.

When the opposing forces became strong enough, the Boeing 777’s breakout mechanism activated. This system is designed to help pilots if one control column jams. But in this case, nothing had jammed.

Even worse, the captain was accidentally transmitting parts of the cockpit struggle over the radio, allowing air traffic control to hear the confusion live.

But the aircraft was not broken.

The Boeing 777 was doing exactly what it had been designed to do.

snippet.title: Air Crash Investigation - Inner City Carnage (S14E08) - [FULL EPISODE]
snippet.description:
On 4 November 2008, an official Mexican Secretariat of the Interior aircraft crashed in central Mexico City at around 18:45 local time. There were sixteen fatalities—all nine people on board and seven people on the ground. The plane, a Learjet 45, was carrying Mexican Secretary of the Interior Juan Camilo Mouriño. The plane crashed in rush-hour traffic close to the intersection of Paseo de la Reforma and the Anillo Periférico, in the Las Lomas business district. During its approach to Mexico City International Airport, the plane followed a Boeing 767 of Mexicana too closely and encountered wake turbulence which caused it to invert into a nose-down position. The pilots were able to reduce the angle of descent, but due to excessive speed and insufficient altitude, were unable to regain control of the aircraft. The plane crashed into a building, exploding on impact and killing 16 people.
